papers.title: Metabolic cost sets the shear stress profile of optimal vascular trees
papers.abstract: Vascular remodeling responds to local wall shear stress, but transport efficiency belongs to the network as a whole. We connect these scales by minimizing dissipation under a fixed maintenance budget, with vessel cost proportional to mass raised to an exponent b. At an optimum, dissipated power is proportional to vessel cost. This yields the shear set point |{tau} | {propto} r^(b-1){ell}^(b-1)/2 for radius r and length {ell}, with uniform shear recovered at b = 1. The associated local adaptation rule decreases the global functional, although the topology it reaches retains a memory of development. Simulations with 400 and 700 sinks show that staged growth improves transport mainly by allowing pruned connections to regrow. Fluctuating demand sustains loops without increasing the maintenance budget. The local condition fixes allocation on a given support, whereas growth and variable demand shape the topology that survives.

papers.title: Polyglutamine aggregation proceeds by stochastic nucleation in the C. elegans nervous system
papers.abstract: Fibrillar protein aggregation is the hallmark of a wide variety of neurodegenerative diseases. It is still poorly understood how soluble proteins transition to fibrillar aggregates, in particular within the complex environment of cells and tissues. Here, we employ the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans to elucidate the molecular mechanisms of polyglutamine aggregation in the nervous system of a multicellular animal. By using fluorescence microscopy in combination with mathematical modelling, we find that polyglutamine aggregation occurs by stochastic nucleation in individual neurons, at a rate that is of the same order of magnitude as previously determined for muscle cells. The J-protein DNAJB6 strongly suppresses polyglutamine aggregation in both tissues, consistent with a mechanism in which aggregation is limited by primary nucleation. We confirm that the same mechanism holds true for a construct including the disease-relevant flanking regions of Huntingtin exon 1. Altogether, our data reveal that polyglutamine aggregation occurs spontaneously and largely independent of the cellular context.

papers.title: Torque-optimized body morphing enables rapid surface to underwater diving in whirligig beetles
papers.abstract: Known for their rapid water surface locomotion, whirligig beetles (Gyrinidae) are also fast divers. They can transition from the surface to underwater swimming in under 100 ms. Diving requires them to generate sufficient hydrodynamic torque to break the water surface and reorient the body. However, the mechanism by which whirligigs create the necessary pitch-down torque is unknown. Here, we show that their diving is achieved by bending the abdomen. The inertial hydrodynamic pressure on the flexed abdomen generates the torque necessary for surface breaking and body rotation. The torque is maximized at an abdominal angle of 45{degrees}, whereas for effective diving, whirligigs display a preferential abdominal angle of around 28{degrees}, closely aligning with the angle that maximizes the torque-to-drag ratio. This abdominal angle is optimized by balancing torque generation with the drag penalty. Our findings inspire a mechanism for surface-to-underwater transition, offering design principles for multimodal robots capable of locomotion across the air-water interface.

papers.title: A Kiss-and-Ride Mechanism for Lipid Exchange at Membrane Contact Sites
papers.abstract: Lipid transfer proteins (LTPs) mediate non-vesicular lipid transport at membrane contact sites, yet how transient membrane tethering contributes to lipid transfer remains poorly understood. Here, we use the single-domain yeast phosphatidylserine transporter Osh6, a member of the oxysterol-binding protein-related protein family, to investigate tethering-dependent lipid transport. We show that Osh6 can access two transport modes depending on membrane composition: conventional shuttling between membranes and a tethering-dependent mode in which the opposing membrane facilitates cargo extraction from the donor membrane. Combining lipid transport and membrane-tethering measurements with kinetic analysis, lipid partitioning, and in vivo complementation, we provide evidence for a transient membrane-bridged intermediate during lipid transfer. Productive phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate (PI4P) extraction destabilizes this bridged state, allowing cargo-loaded Osh6 to disengage and continue the transport cycle. We term this mechanism kiss-and-ride, in which transient membrane contact facilitates cargo extraction ("kiss") before the cargo-loaded protein disengages ("ride"). Consistent with this model, PI4P transport is preserved in a lidless Osh6 mutant with impaired membrane dissociation, whereas phosphatidylserine transport is strongly reduced, revealing distinct mechanistic requirements for the two cargoes. Together, our findings reveal a tethering-dependent transport mode in a cup-like LTP and suggest that membrane contact sites can actively shape the mechanism of lipid transport rather than merely bringing donor and acceptor membranes into proximity.

papers.title: State-selective nanobodies to probe Guanylate-binding protein coat assembly and function
papers.abstract: Cell-autonomous immunity against gram-negative bacterial pathogens relies on Guanylate-binding proteins (GBPs). GBPs are interferon-inducible guanosine triphosphate hydrolases that coat cytosolic bacteria and promote non-canonical inflammasome activation. GBP coat assembly is initiated by GBP1, which binds bacterial lipopolysaccharide and recruits further paralogs in a hierarchical and nucleotide-dependent manner. Dissecting the contributions of individual GBPs has remained challenging because the seven human paralogs are structurally similar and undergo nucleotide-driven conformational changes that are difficult to resolve in cellular and biochemical experiments. Here, we developed a nanobody toolbox for the state-selective probing of human GBP coat assembly. We identify eight nanobodies with distinct paralog, domain, and conformational specificities and define their binding profiles and epitopes using complementary biophysical assays and cryogenic electron microscopy. We further demonstrate the utility of selected nanobodies by demonstrating their functionality in membrane reconstitution assays and in infected cells. A dimer-disrupting nanobody blocks progression of GBP-coat assembly from soluble GBP1 assemblies to LPS-associated coats, suggesting a stage-specific structural transition during coat formation. In contrast, a dimer selective nanobody binds assembled coats without measurably perturbing their organisation and is robustly recruited to GBP1-positive bacteria in infected cells, indicating that this dimer interface remains intact and accessible in coat-associated GBP1. Together, these nanobodies establish a set of state-selective reagents to distinguish, perturb, and probe GBP assemblies in structural, biochemical, and cellular studies

papers.title: Red states modulate energy localization between the antenna and trap in PSI
papers.abstract: The core antenna of the photosystem I (PSI) complex of oxygenic photosynthesis operates at near perfect quantum efficiency, making it one of the most efficient energy conversation devices in nature. The presence of low energy or red chlorophylls (chls) is nearly universal in this core antenna, and these red chls are known to extend the light harvesting capacity and control the rate of energy migration in PSI. Surprisingly, the significance of the structural position of the red chls in PSI remains unknown. In this study, we introduced mutations that generate specific red sites in the PSI core antenna, consistent with those observed in natural species. Using CryoEM, we characterized the structural changes at these red sites. Using transient absorption spectroscopy, we measured the effects of red chlorophyll at specific sites on energy transfer and trapping in PSI to identify their functional significance. While one site funneled energy to the reaction center, the other slowed equilibration in the antenna. These opposing effects indicate different functions are associated with the different red chlorophyll location, reconciling previous seemingly incompatible suggestions as to their functional role.

papers.title: Generating Structural Ensembles of Disordered Proteins with Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Generative models of protein structures have accelerated scientific discovery. However, the leading structure-prediction models are trained primarily on crystal structures, limiting their ability to sample the conformations of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs). All-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can probe the diversity of IDP conformational ensembles, but these simulations are slow and costly. Leveraging the speed of generative models and the accuracy of MD, we develop Zephyr, an SE(3) equivariant diffusion model trained on simulated IDP ensembles. The model generates the structure of a single protein sequence in two phases: a coarse-grained structure is first sampled and heavy atoms are subsequently denoised onto this structure. We evaluate our method on two fronts: ensemble accuracy and sampling efficiency. Across five test systems, the model reproduces key geometric and energetic metrics of the MD ensembles, while sampling at least 63 times faster.

papers.title: A Nanomechanical Fingerprint of Centromeric Methylation Co-Localization in TNBC Chromosomal Instability
papers.abstract: Centromeric heterochromatin is maintained by a self-reinforcing loop between DNA methylation (5mC) and histone H3 lysine 9 trimethylation (H3K9me3), yet whether this coupling is preserved at the level of individual chromosomes in cancer has been inaccessible to conventional epigenomic assays, which average signals across cell populations and cannot resolve single-chromosome heterogeneity. Here, we use antibody-functionalized atomic force spectroscopy to simultaneously map 5mC and H3K9me3 at the centromeres of individual metaphase chromosomes from non-tumorigenic, luminal, and triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) cell models. Co-localized 5mC/H3K9me3 sites are mechanically stiffer than sites carrying either mark alone across the panel, revealing a cooperative biophysical signature of epigenetic crosstalk. Luminal chromosomes acquire the highest mark density, co-localization, and stiffness, whereas TNBC chromosomes show reduced density and diminished, though not absent, co-localization and stiffness, converging toward the low baseline of non-tumorigenic epithelium. TGF-{beta}1-induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition reproduces this attenuated phenotype in luminal cells, linking it directly to a process central to TNBC aggressiveness. These biophysical parameters classify cancer versus non-tumorigenic chromosomes with near-perfect, cross-validated accuracy, and further resolve the two TNBC subtypes using colocalization-derived features alone (macro-F1 = 0.933). These results establish the mechanical consequence of epigenetic mark co-localization as a single-chromosome-resolvable signature of centromeric organization, attenuated in aggressive breast cancer, and demonstrate a force-spectroscopy platform for mechano-epigenetic profiling of cancer chromosomes.

papers.title: Plunge freezing tweezers with ultrasonic excitation for reducing preferred particle orientation in cryo-EM
papers.abstract: Preferred particle orientation, which results from the adsorption of proteins to the air-water interface, is a frequently encountered issue in single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). Particles then present only a limited number of views, which are oversampled during data acquisition at the expense of throughput, while other views may be missing altogether. In severe cases, a high-resolution reconstruction becomes unattainable. We have recently established that ultrasonic excitation of the sample during vitrification improves the angular distribution by detaching particles from the air-water interface and reshuffling their orientations. Here, we describe an implementation of this principle for a plunge freezing apparatus, in which the ultrasonic transducer is integrated into the head of the pair of tweezers holding the sample, and show that this design is able to reduce preferred orientation. We demonstrate this for hemagglutinin, the canonical example of preferred orientation, and show that the fraction of side and tilted views increases with the excitation amplitude. This allows us to obtain a complete reconstruction of the trimer at 2.5 [A].

papers.title: Complex folding kinetics of multi-domain proteins disentangled with periodic forces by magnetic tweezers
papers.abstract: Force spectroscopy yields direct access to the interplay between free energy and transition kinetics of proteins and nucleic acids. Yet, complex molecules such as multi-domain proteins exhibit multiple intermediates during unfolding and refolding with different or similar stabilities and kinetics ranging from milliseconds to hours. In particular, conditions at equilibrium or near equilibrium are often impossible to find for multi-domain systems and traditional out-of-equilibrium experiments challenging to analyze. Here, we propose periodic forces to bridge different stabilities, selectively enhance intermediate populations, and a rigorous analysis framework to disentangle kinetics of multi-domain protein folding at quasi-equilibrium. Using high resolution magnetic tweezers, we apply well-defined periodic square functions of force with steady states that can be flexibly modulated. We demonstrate the analysis framework with a well-studied simple model system, the two-state folder {lambda}6-85. We show that periodic force experiments reproduce equilibrium kinetics and a simple theoretical framework opens the possibility to expand periodic force measurements to complex multidomain proteins. We apply the framework to the multi-domain protein mimic (Protein L)x8 and show how periodic forces can enhance populations of distinct intermediate states by tuning their frequency and amplitude. In a last example, we show how to dissect entangled states of a hybrid two-domain protein termed {lambda}-L, where 100-fold difference in kinetics of both domains would prevent equilibrium analysis. Expanding a two-state to a three-state periodic force protocol allowed for directed population of folding intermediates. We anticipate our method and analysis framework will expand the possibilities to decipher complex multi-domain folds and their multi-dimensional folding pathways.

papers.title: Conformational dynamics of ND2 antiporter-like subunit in intact and truncated complex I
papers.abstract: Respiratory complex I is a large redox-driven proton pump and contributes to the proton motive force required for ATP generation in mitochondria and bacteria. It has been extensively studied with structural and biochemical approaches leading to enhanced understanding of its three- dimensional architecture. Despite significant progress in deciphering its catalytic function, the redox-coupled proton pumping mechanism remains unclear and extensively debated. The three membrane-bound antiporter-like subunits ND2, ND4 and ND5 are responsible for pumping protons from the negatively charged side (N-side) of the membrane to the positively charged side (P-side). Emerging evidence supports the role of ND5 subunit in releasing pumped protons to the P-side of the membrane, but the question whether ND2 and ND4 also contribute to proton release remains unanswered. Here, we performed atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of an intact and a truncated model of complex I in which ND5 and ND4 subunits are removed in-silico. The simulation data reveals a previously unobserved conformational change in the P-side region of ND2 subunit that occurs much more easily in a truncated model of complex I, as also estimated based on free energy calculations. The conformational change, in part triggered by the artificial exposure of ND2 subunit to lipid bilayer, results in a local hydration of the region, similar to what has been observed in recent cryo-EM structure of plant CI:CIII2 supercomplex. We discuss the functional relevance of observed conformational transitions and identify residues that can be manipulated with biochemical approaches to shed light on proton pumping by complex I.

papers.title: Integrating cell-state and enhancer constraints discriminates models of PU.1 regulation during hematopoietic differentiation
papers.abstract: Distinct PU.1 levels are associated with progenitor, B-cell, and macrophage states during hematopoietic differentiation. A previous dynamical-systems model attributed these levels to multistability generated by PU.1 autoregulation coupled to feedback between PU.1 abundance and cell-cycle progression, but its predictions were not quantitatively evaluated against the motivating measurements. Here, we test this mechanism using reported measurements of PU.1 abundance, its synthesis rate, and cell-cycle duration, and develop progressively more mechanistic alternatives. The original growth-feedback model neither represents the two reported progenitor groups nor reproduces the nonmonotonic relationship between PU.1 abundance and cell-cycle length. Even with experimentally measured cell-type-specific growth rates, PU.1 autoregulation alone does not reproduce the observed PU.1 abundance and synthesis rates across cell states. Reproducing the cell-state measurements requires an additional cell-state-dependent input to PU.1 production. Guided by enhancer regulation, we model positive feedback between PU.1 and C/EBP and constrain it with reporter measurements, but this architecture cannot jointly reproduce the reporter and cell-state datasets. Adding RUNX1 permits data-consistent stable states when high effective cooperativity in PU.1-dependent C/EBP activation is allowed. Thus, combined dynamical and cis-regulatory constraints support additional regulation of PU.1 production beyond autoregulation, cell-type-specific dilution, and C/EBP feedback. The RUNX1-extended architecture provides one biologically grounded realization and generates experimentally testable hypotheses for differentiation networks.

papers.title: Gag proteolysis drives HIV-1 envelope conformational closure through the gp41 cytoplasmic tail
papers.abstract: HIV-1 must present a fusion-competent envelope glycoprotein (Env) to enter host cells while concealing the very conformation targeted by broadly neutralising antibodies (bnAbs). How the virus resolves this conflict has remained unclear. Using a minimally invasive nanobody-labelling strategy targeting Env's V4 loop, we combine single-virus FRET, fluorescence lifetime cross-correlation spectroscopy, and DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy to resolve Env conformation on individual, intact virions from the primary isolate JR-FL. We show that immature virions predominantly display an open Env conformation, while Gag maturation drives acquisition of the tightly closed, fusion-competent State 1 that harbours the principal bnAb epitope. Truncating the Env cytoplasmic tail abolishes this regulation, identifying the gp41 tail as the conduit linking Gag lattice maturation to Env's conformational fate. We further show that bnAb b12 preferentially binds open Env on immature virions, supporting a decoy mechanism that shields mature virions from immune recognition, with direct implications for HIV-1 vaccine design.

papers.title: Structural basis of selective phospholipid recognition and local membrane deformation by CTL1
papers.abstract: The physiological function of the human choline transporter-like protein CTL1 (SLC44A1) remains elusive despite its implication in key pathophysiological processes. Here we combine cryo-electron microscopy, native mass spectrometry, lipidomics, molecular dynamics simulations and functional assays to characterise the molecular basis of phospholipid recognition by CTL1 and explore its potential molecular role. High-resolution structures of CTL1 in both monomeric and dimeric states reveal a broad amphipathic cavity and an extracellular domain that accommodate multiple phospholipid species, identifying phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylserine, phosphatidylinositol and phosphatidic acid as endogenous CTL1 ligands. Molecular dynamics simulations show spontaneous phospholipid recruitment into these conserved binding sites accompanied by membrane thinning, curvature and local phospholipid reorganisation, with membrane deformation being enhanced upon dimerisation. Functional analyses in mammalian cells and in reconstituted proteoliposomes failed to detect CTL1-mediated choline transport, supporting a function distinct from canonical choline uptake. Together, our findings suggest that CTL1 acts as a phospholipid-binding protein capable of locally deforming the membrane and provide a structural framework linking phospholipid recognition to membrane organisation. These results offer new insights into potential mechanisms underlying the altered phospholipid homeostasis associated with CTL1 dysfunction in neurological diseases and cancer.

papers.title: Shear Strain Stiffening in Cartilage is Governed by a Mechanical Phase Transition
papers.abstract: Large shear deformation in cartilage can lead to tissue failure and injury, which are often precursors to diseases such as post-traumatic osteoarthritis. Under shear, cartilage strain-stiffens prior to failure, which makes stiffening an important indicator of changes to the loading of the extracellular matrix that gives rise to this tissue's properties. While a variety of stiffening mechanisms ranging from uncrimping to fiber-alignment have been explored, whether such mechanisms apply to the depth dependent shear strain stiffening in articular cartilage remains poorly understood. Here, we present experiments and theory that support the idea that the strain-stiffening behavior is caused by a mechanical phase transition from a random isotropic network whose mechanics arise primarily from bending-dominated modes to one where the mechanics arise from stretching-dominated modes. Indeed, consistent with network model predictions, we find that stress-strain data for all depths can be collapsed onto a single universal curve that diverges at a depth-dependent critical strain. These results show that increasing the local concentration of collagen, which constitutes the primary load-bearing network in cartilage, decreases the critical strain at which the strain-stiffening transition occurs, while increasing the low-strain elastic modulus. Furthermore, we demonstrate that bulk compression leads to a higher critical strain and decreased low-strain elastic modulus. Network simulations capture this rich behavior, and indicate that under compression the network collapses, which allows for larger strains before the transition from bending-dominated to stretching-dominated mechanics occurs. Collectively, these findings shed light on the roles that tissue composition and axial strain play in the mechanisms that organize how articular cartilage stiffens during the lead-up to injury.

papers.title: Cellular Density Homeostasis Is Governed by an Anisotropic Attractor and Predictive Feedback Control
papers.abstract: Cell density is a fundamental biophysical property of living cells, yet the dynamical architecture underlying density homeostasis remains unknown. Here, we reconstruct the geometry, dynamics, and control structure governing cellular density regulation from single-cell mass-volume measurements acquired during recovery from osmotic perturbation. We identify a persistent anisotropic attractor in mass-volume state space that permits coordinated density-preserving fluctuations while strongly suppressing density-changing deviations. Optimal transport analysis reveals directed recovery trajectories confined to this attractor, enabling inference of an effective density-restoring control law. Density deviations are associated with coordinated changes in biomass accumulation and volume expansion that together generate an effective density-restoring control law. Moreover, density error contains significant predictive information regarding future corrective behavior, revealing an information-rich component of cellular regulation. Together, these findings establish cellular density homeostasis as an emergent dynamical control process and demonstrate how attractor reconstruction, optimal transport, and information theory can be combined to uncover the organizing principles of biological homeostasis.

papers.title: Interplay of mechanics, growth and viral infection dynamics in a spatially expanding bacterial colony
papers.abstract: We investigate the dynamics of the spread of the infection due to a phage- during the range expansion of an E coli colony. We find a rich panoply of spatio-temporal dynamics at large colony-level length scales, arising due to the interplay of mechanical forces, growth and viral infection dynamics at smaller cellular length scales. Strikingly, the phages "surf" the front of the growing bacterial colony by hitchhiking on E coli that are advected due to the growth of bacteria in the colony, resulting in an anisotropic spread of the phages. We identify microscopic processes - of the phage release during lysis (occurring on short millisecond timescales at length scales close to that of a single bacterium) and local nematic alignment of the rod-like E coli bacteria (occurring on timescales comparable to the bacterial growth rate and the length scales of a few bacterial cells) - that enhance the advective effects driving the hitchhiking behavior. Combining our experiments with a mathematical model, we explain the multiple spatio-temporal dynamical regimes - from the coexistence of uninfected bacteria, resistant (lysogenic) cells and phages, to fixed points where the entire population turns resistant or remains uninfected. Our work broaches a new frontier in the investigation of eco-evolutionary processes arising from the mechanical and ecological forces due to the interactions between viruses and their hosts.

papers.title: Simulating Bead-Tethered Biomolecules: Force-Probe Coupled Steered Molecular Dynamics (fp-SMD) in Optical Tweezers Force Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Interpreting single-molecule force spectroscopy (SMFS) data from optical tweezers with steered molecular dynamics (SMD) is hindered by a severe timescale mismatch: SMD trajectories span nanoseconds to microseconds, while SMFS experiments unfold over milliseconds to seconds, forcing SMD to pull six to nine orders of magnitude faster than experiment and systematically distorting rupture forces, molecular pathways, and kinetic intermediates. We introduce force-probe coupled steered molecular dynamics (fp-SMD), which explicitly propagates the force probe (the optically trapped bead) alongside the biomolecule within a single classical Hamiltonian description of the coupled molecule-linker-bead system. A Predict-Correct Trajectory Propagation (PCTP) scheme resolves the resulting computational bottleneck by decoupling the fast molecular relaxation from the slow, macroscopic bead motion, using metadynamics and transition-state theory to identify the kinetically resolved molecular intermediate reached at each macroscopic time step. On the cholesterol-{beta}-cyclodextrin ({beta}-CD) host-guest complex, fp-SMD reproduces the experimental rupture-force histogram directly at matched conditions, without extrapolation from standard SMD. fp-SMD further resolves how applied force reshapes the molecular escape pathway itself--cholesterol dissociates via a high-angle route at low force and a direct, small-angle route at high force--providing, to our knowledge, the first direct structural evidence for force-induced pathway switching within small host-guest systems believed to underlie catch-slip bond behavior. fp-SMD/PCTP thus offers a general route to simulating force-probe-coupled biomolecular mechanics at experimentally relevant timescales.

papers.title: Multi-Chain Hamiltonian Replica Exchange Framework for Probing Transient Helices and Order-Disorder Transitions in Proteins
papers.abstract: Simulations have emerged as a pillar in biophysics to understand behavior at the molecular scale, in particular for proteins such as intrinsically disordered proteins. These often show transient folding with long-lived states that are challenging to efficiently sample using conventional simulations. Here, we show that Hamiltonian replica-exchange at the level of hydrogen bonds can be used to systematically explore the conformational landscape of proteins. Investigating the IM30 protein, a partially alpha helical protein, under the PLUM coarse-grain force-field, we show that this approach straightforwardly allows characterization of local helix stability, which would be otherwise hard to obtain. For instance, we show that some regions of the conserved coiled-coil structure are less stable than others. By combining the different replicas with principal component analysis, we are able to dissect the conformational landscape of the IM30 protein. Taken together, this indicates that enhanced sampling remains an important part of simulations, allowing insights that cannot be easily obtained in traditional simulations.

papers.title: pH-sensitive binder design with Proton-PottsMPNN
papers.abstract: Physiological compartments span a wide pH range, from blood plasma near pH 7.4 through the mildly acidic tumor microenvironment to the acidified endosome and lysosome, and binders whose affinity responds to these differences underpin recycling antibodies, catalytic extracellular degraders and tumor-conditional therapeutics. Such binders are still obtained mainly by combinatorial histidine scanning and display selection, which is laborious and yields few transferable design rules. Recent computational approaches have enabled the design of pH-sensitive binders that engage at physiological pH and release under acidic conditions, by introducing histidines at key positions so that protonation generates electrostatic repulsion, evaluated through physics-based calculations. However, because the design model has no explicit representation of protonation state, it cannot shape the residues around a titratable site to favor one state over the other, leaving pH sensitivity to be screened for rather than specified. Here we present Proton-PottsMPNN, a sequence-design model that explicitly represents the protonated and deprotonated states of histidine, aspartate and glutamate as distinct sequence tokens. Because protonation state is specified rather than inferred, the model redesigns the microenvironment around a titratable residue so that the chosen protonation state is energetically favored over its alternative. Using Proton-PottsMPNN we designed a library of 8,407 de novo PD-L1 candidate binders in which sequence-structure compatibility and protonation state preference were designed jointly under a single energy function, with no structure-prediction filtering applied. The full library was synthesized and displayed on yeast, then screened against PD-L1 across a series of pH values by fluorescence- and magnetic-activated cell sorting, recovering 237 and 288 unique pH-dependent designs respectively. Transition pH values spanned 4.0 to 5.8, and switches were centered on protonated aspartate and glutamate as well as histidine. Recovered designs showed a stronger model preference for their designed protonation state than designs from the same backbone that were not recovered, and this preference was strongest in the designs that required the most acidic conditions to bind. Proton-PottsMPNN therefore designs binders that engage PD-L1 under acidic conditions fully de novo, directly from a specified protonation state.

papers.title: Two functionally distinct amyloid-β intermediates link aggregation pathways to pathology in Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: Neurotoxic intermediates formed during amyloid-{beta}(A{beta}) aggregation are thought to drive Alzheimer's disease, yet their rarity and transient nature have obscured their identity and formation pathways in the human brain. Here, we combine super-resolution microscopy and single-molecule functional imaging with kinetic modelling to classify A{beta} intermediates according to their membrane-disrupting activity and connect their damaging effects to the aggregation pathways that generate them. Applying this framework to recombinant A{beta}42, an Alzheimer's knock-in mouse model and human Alzheimer's brain tissue, we find two functionally distinct intermediate populations present across all systems. They form through separate aggregation routes and differ in their neurotoxicity, abundance and susceptibility to inhibition. Both damage neurons and glia, but only one converts into plaques. Suppressing these intermediates pharmacologically in mice reduces plaque burden, attenuates astrogliosis and improves cognition. Our findings connect model systems with human pathology and identify intermediate formation pathways as actionable therapeutic targets across protein-misfolding disorders.

papers.title: Network analysis of correlated conformational dynamics across the evolution of influenza A virus NS1
papers.abstract: Protein evolution requires sequence changes to alter molecular properties without disrupting the dynamic organization necessary for function. How residue-level networks of correlated motions accommodate such mutations remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the evolution of correlated conformational dynamics in nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) variants of influenza A viruses that emerged between 1918 and 2004. From molecular dynamics (MD) simulations we built residue networks in which edge weights reflect generalized correlations of conformational motion. The network of correlated dynamics is characterized using centrality analysis. Overall network properties are well-conserved across NS1 variants, indicating evolutionary robustness of the dynamical network. Residues ranked highly across multiple centrality measures form a predominantly hydrophobic cluster in the protein core. These residues exhibited low conformational entropy and high sequence conservation, consistent with rigid, coordinated motions. In contrast, residues exhibiting large differences in betweenness and closeness centrality ranks occupied flexible, solvent-exposed regions surrounding the core network. These residues also showed lower evolutionary conservation. These findings reveal a core-periphery structure in which a rigid hydrophobic network enables long-range dynamic connectivity while more adaptable peripheral regions accommodate evolutionary sequence variation. This architecture provides a mechanistic framework for long-range epistatic interactions without compromising the underlying structural framework.

papers.title: SMartini: automated small molecule parametrization for Martini 3 force field
papers.abstract: We present SMartini, an automated pipeline for deriving Martini 3 coarse-grained force-field parameters for arbitrary small molecules. Starting from a molecular structure or a SMILES string, the pipeline maps the all-atom molecule onto a coarse-grained bead representation and automatically fits both bonded and non-bonded parameters. Bonded parameters are obtained via Boltzmann inversion of atomistic molecular dynamics trajectories; successive rounds of coarse-grained simulation and distribution-matching updates then refine these estimates until the coarse-grained conformational ensemble reproduces the all-atom reference within tolerance. We validate the pipeline on a diverse set of small molecules including drug-like compounds, metabolites, and cofactors. Implemented as a modular sequence of scripts that can be orchestrated on high-performance computing clusters, SMartini makes automated parametrization of large ligand libraries practical and reduces the manual effort required for coarse-grained model development, enabling high-throughput coarse-grained simulations of protein--ligand systems within the Martini 3 ecosystem

papers.title: Core NHEJ Factors Maintain Synapsis Across Diverse DNA End Structures
papers.abstract: DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) generated by genotoxic stress frequently contain chemically diverse termini that require end processing before ligation by non-homologous end joining (NHEJ). How end chemistry influences assembly and persistence of NHEJ synaptic complexes remains unclear. Using single-molecule imaging approaches in Xenopus egg extract, we measured formation and stability of the long-range (LRC) and short-range (SRC) complexes on nine DNA substrates spanning kinase-, polymerase- and nuclease-dependent processing requirements. LRC formation and lifetime were comparable across end types, and SRC formation and stability were largely insensitive to end chemistry. DNA hairpins, physiological intermediates of V(D)J recombination, were a notable exception that formed LRCs but inefficiently transitioned to SRCs. Depletion of cognate processing factors had modest effects on SRC formation and persistence, indicating that core NHEJ factors provide the principal structural support for synapsis across diverse termini. Although XLF was required for SRC formation on all substrates, reducing an XLF dimer from two intact tail/Ku-binding motifs to one selectively reduced productive SRC formation on ends requiring processing. Together, these results support a model in which partially redundant protein-protein interactions between core NHEJ factors maintain synapsis while end-specific processing reactions shape repair outcome.

papers.title: SOP-Multi-π: A Two-Site Coarse-Grained Model with Rescaled Aromatic Interactions to Bridge Single-Chain Ensembles and Condensate Phase Behavior of IDPs and Multidomain Proteins
papers.abstract: We present SOP-Multi-{pi}, an enhanced version of the two-bead-per-amino-acid resolution Self-Organized Polymer (SOP) model designed to investigate the conformational dynamics of Intrinsically Disordered Proteins (IDPs) and their phase behavior in biomolecular condensates. The original SOP-IDP and SOP-Multi models work well for chains in good solvents that predominantly adopt expanded conformations. However, they fail to reproduce the single-chain properties and phase-separation behavior of IDPs such as hnRNPA1 and its variants, which have a distinct pattern of aromatic residues. We therefore reparameterized the SOP-IDP force field to explicitly capture {pi}-{pi} and cation-{pi} interactions at the coarse-grained (CG) resolution. These interactions are weak but important for biomolecular recognition and for driving and stabilizing biomolecular condensates. Dimensionless rescaling prefactors ({lambda}) were applied exclusively to the aromatic {pi}-{pi} (Phe, Tyr, Trp) and cation-{pi} (Arg/Lys with Phe, Tyr, Trp) pairs. They were optimized iteratively against experimental radii of gyration of the hnRNPA1 low-complexity domain (A1-LCD) and its 16 aromatic and charge mutants. This restored a physically meaningful Tyr > Phe interaction hierarchy, and the Pearson correlation for Rg improved from r = 0.07 (SOP-IDP) to r = 0.83 (RMSD = 0.08 nm). The same parameters, without further tuning, gave r = 0.93 for 34 additional IDPs (24-198 residues) and reproduced Flory scaling ( {nu} ~ 0.588). We back-mapped microsecond-scale CG ensembles to all-atom representations and computed SAXS and Kratky profiles for direct comparison with experiments on IDPs and on the multidomain proteins hnRNPA1, TDP-43, G3BP1, and FUS. In direct-coexistence slab simulations, the model captures the phase behavior of A1-LCD condensates and their variants, with critical temperatures that correlate strongly with experiment (r = 0.88) but are somewhat underestimated in absolute terms. The model is implemented in LAMMPS, and a detailed user manual is provided for setting up single-chain and multi-chain condensate simulations of full-length multidomain proteins.

papers.title: Long-range transport of biomolecular condensates by Marangoni effect
papers.abstract: How mesoscale cargos such as biomolecular condensates are transported and spatially positioned within cells remains a fundamental question in cell biology. During Caenorhabditis elegans zygote polarization, a substantial fraction of P granules undergoes persistent anterior-to-posterior motion that cannot be fully explained by dissolution-recondensation. Here, combining microfluidic reconstitution, quantitative micropipette aspiration and live-cell imaging, we show that a MEG-3 concentration gradient generates interfacial-tension asymmetry and drives the directed transport of PGL-3-RNA co-condensates in vitro and P granules in vivo through the Marangoni effect. This framework enables parameter-free quantitative predictions of condensate transport. Orthogonal molecular perturbations abolish or reverse directional migration, directly linking interfacial properties to transport behavior and establishing the specificity of this mechanism. Together, our findings identify the Marangoni effect as a previously unrecognized mechanism for intracellular transport of biomolecular condensates and provide direct causal evidence that condensate emergent properties can contribute to physiological organization.

papers.title: A Dynamics-Informed Machine Learning Framework for Inhibitor Optimization Against Quickly Evolving Targets to Avoid Resistance
papers.abstract: Drug resistance often emerges through mutations that reshape protein conformational ensembles, allowing inhibitor potency to be altered without directly disrupting protein-ligand contacts. Consequently, the molecular mechanisms underlying these effects remain difficult to identify, hindering the design of inhibitors with durable potency against rapidly evolving drug targets. To address this challenge, we developed ROBUST, a physics-informed machine learning framework that integrates experimental measurements, molecular dynamics simulations, and interpretable statistical modeling to identify energetic determinants of inhibitor potency. Using HIV-1 protease as a stringent model system for drug resistance, we determined 157 new inhibition constants and integrated them with prior measurements to establish a comprehensive experimental dataset of 364 protease-inhibitor pairs. Analysis of the corresponding molecular dynamics simulations revealed a compact network of energetic interactions that quantitatively explains how resistance mutations and inhibitor modifications jointly reshape molecular recognition and inhibitor potency across the multidimensional resistance landscape. Models constructed from these energetic signatures predicted binding free energies with high accuracy (RMSE < 1 kcal mol-1) and successfully generalized to unseen darunavir analogs. Importantly, ROBUST accurately prioritized unseen analogs based on their potency across the variant set, demonstrating its utility for identifying compounds with improved resistance profiles. Together, these results uncover the energetic principles through which resistance mutations and inhibitor modifications alter potency and establish ROBUST as a mechanistically interpretable framework for translating these insights into resistance-aware inhibitor optimization against rapidly evolving drug targets.

papers.title: The molecular structural basis of the braking action of muscle
papers.abstract: Skeletal muscles generate force and shortening through a structural powerstroke in actin-bound myosin motors linked to ATP hydrolysis, but they also act as brakes to resist stretching by an external load. The molecular structural basis of muscle braking has remained obscure. Here we show that muscle braking is driven both by structural changes in myosin motors and by distortion of the lattice of thick and thin filaments including their M-band and Z-disk connections. A strained motor conformation is established early during stretch, but force continues to increase as thin filaments are displaced from their symmetrical lattice positions, the lateral shear between thick filaments increases, and the lattice volume decreases. Moreover, whilst the motor conformation rapidly recovers after the stretch, the distortion of the filament lattice is largely maintained, storing the work done on the muscle during stretch and accounting for the residual force enhancement after stretch.

papers.title: Sequential Design of Experiments enables accessible and efficient multidimensional mapping of single- and multi-protein condensates
papers.abstract: Biomolecular condensation emerges from networks of multivalent interactions that respond collectively to molecular composition and environmental conditions. Here, we establish a sequential Design of Experiments (DoE) framework to systematically and efficiently characterise multidimensional condensation landscapes. Applied to three RNA-binding condensate proteins - Dhh1, Ded1 and PGL-3 - the workflow revealed unexpected protein-specific interactions between biophysical and biochemical variables, including RNA, pH and ionic strength, and uncovered context-dependent switch-like behaviours. Extending the framework to protein mixtures revealed how proteins affected each other's condensation and whether they formed condensate-within-condensate structures under different experimental conditions. Finally, an unexpected response identified by DoE prompted mechanistic analysis of Dhh1, revealing an ATP-independent RNA-binding surface that promotes efficient condensation in vitro and contributes to P-body formation in cells. Sequential DoE therefore provides an experimentally accessible strategy for uncovering context-dependent condensate regulation and converting multidimensional response patterns into mechanistic hypotheses.

papers.title: Structural basis of phosphatidylserine enhancement of Gas6 ligand-induced Axl activation
papers.abstract: TAMs (Tyro3, Axl, and MerTK) are receptor tyrosine kinases with primary roles in apoptotic clearance and immune suppression. In apoptosis, bridging complexes form between TAM receptors on phagocytic cells and TAM ligand bound to phosphatidylserine exposed on the surface of dying cells, but how these complexes form or why lipid is required for receptor activation is poorly understood. We present the first structures of a complete TAM receptor (Axl) and ligand (Gas6) 2:2 bridging complex with and without lipid, which suggest that the lipid functions to stabilize and promote active complexes. We also observe a stable 1:1 complex, presumed to be inactive, and provide evidence that these complexes are conversely able to form higher-order oligomers. We propose a mechanism for how lipids promote TAM receptor activation, providing a structural and biochemical basis for developing therapies that selectively target the lipid-dependent, immunosuppressive arm of TAM signaling exploited by tumors.
